comparator.name: Applied Physics
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 regulations specify 60 EC per year, including the Applied Physics deepening minor, three restricted course choices and a 15 EC research project.
components: Builds on Calculus 1. Introduces differential equations and Fourier methods for physical problems.
Uses knowledge from the introductory lab, mechanics, and electricity and magnetism to plan and carry out an experiment.
Builds on the two first-year physics labs. The second advanced laboratory course follows in year three.
Applied Physics & Society: Ethical and Professional Aspects
Compulsory atomic and condensed-matter physics course.
Compulsory control-engineering course deemed appropriate for bachelor Applied Physics.
One of three 5 EC choices. This example shows Atoms and Molecules, which builds on quantum physics.
This example shows Principles of Measurement Systems, which draws on circuits, electronics and experimental uncertainty.
This example shows Nanoprobing and Nanofabrication, which builds on solid-state physics.

Normally requires 150 EC in Applied Physics. Third-year students who earn at least 135 EC within their first three years of registration may also start. Students complete an individual project, report and presentation.

core: Fundamental and applied physics, experimental laboratories, materials, devices and instrumentation
Calculus, linear algebra, differential equations, numerical methods, probability, signals and physical-system models
Scientific programming, data analysis, image processing, algorithms and computational prediction
Technical-system design, control, product development and technological innovation
adjacent: Renewable-energy technologies, natural physical systems and sustainable resource applications
Medical technologies, imaging and quantitative study of living systems
Advanced materials, nanoscale systems and nanotechnology
questions: How can mathematical and computational models describe and predict complex physical or living systems?
How can physical principles and quantitative evidence inform technical, energy and medical applications?

candidates.label: Natural physical systems, resources and renewable energy
Medical technologies, imaging and living systems
Advanced materials and nanotechnology
candidates.reason: UCR has sustainability materials context and resource-recovery applications, but no condensed-matter, materials-physics, device-physics, nanofabrication or experimental characterisation sequence from which a coherent 24-course materials or nanotechnology programme could be built.

selection.assessment: The first option applies mathematics and computing to autonomous systems. The second uses quantitative and experimental methods for Earth and energy systems. The third applies imaging, signals and modelling to living systems. Materials and nanotechnology would require more sustained training in solid-state physics and fabrication.

alternatives.label: Mathematical modelling, autonomous systems & energy technology
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by mathematics, programming, algorithms, data, imaging, optimisation, machine learning and robotics, with a bounded energy-technology strand. The label does not claim mechanics, electromagnetism, quantum, materials, device or experimental-physics formation.
alternatives.concept: Model how systems change and how robots sense and act. Use calculus, numerical methods, signals and computer vision to investigate technical problems, and apply modelling and design to renewable energy.
progression: Programming precedes algorithms and decisions under uncertainty. Mathematical Methods and Linear Algebra prepare for numerical methods, signals and robotics. Machine Learning precedes neural networks.

alternatives.label: Mathematical modelling, Earth systems & sustainable technology
alternatives.labelReason: Six Earth and environmental courses replace six specialist algorithmic courses, producing a natural-system, resource and energy curriculum while keeping quantitative modelling central. The label does not imply geophysics or Applied Physics equivalence.
alternatives.concept: Use mathematical models and measurements to study Earth systems and sustainable technologies. Combine geophysics, water and mineral chemistry, resource recovery and renewable-energy design.
progression: Sustainability and Earth-science foundations precede field measurements, geochemistry and recovery experiments. Energy & Sustainability and Sustainability Essentials II precede Renewable System Design.
alternatives.distinctness: Six courses, or 45 EC, differ in each direction. Optimisation, computer networks, algorithms, advanced algorithms, AI decision-making and reinforcement learning are replaced by Earth-system modelling, Dynamic Earth, soils and aquifers, environmental biogeochemistry, resource recovery and advanced resource research. These changes implement a natural physical-systems direction rather than threshold-filling substitutions.

alternatives.label: Biomedical systems, imaging & quantitative modelling
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum contains a sustained molecular, physiological, neurobiological, laboratory and disease-science core alongside mathematics, programming, imaging and data modelling. It does not claim medical physics, physical instrumentation or professional clinical preparation.
alternatives.concept: Use mathematics and computation to study human and living systems. Combine anatomy, physiology and laboratory science with image analysis, signals, robotics and statistical modelling.
progression: Programming and mathematics precede quantitative modelling and robotics. Brain and behaviour prepares for advanced cognition. Life-science foundations lead into physiology, pathology and laboratory work.
alternatives.distinctness: Against the autonomous-systems route, fourteen courses (105 EC) differ in each direction; against the Earth-and-energy route, thirteen courses (97.5 EC) differ in each direction. The third programme replaces most specialist algorithms, autonomy, Earth, resource and energy study with molecular, physiological, neurobiological, laboratory and disease science, as required by the medical-technology direction.

implements regression and statistical-learning methods for biological and clinical data
studies numerical image processing, feature detection and tracking relevant to medical imaging without claiming physical instrumentation
develops neural-network and deep-learning models for advanced biomedical data and image analysis

notes.text: The UCR options share methods in mathematics, computing, signals and experimental analysis. Groningen also requires a sustained physics sequence in mechanics, electromagnetism, quantum and thermal physics, with specialist laboratories, instrumentation and an individual Applied Physics research project.

blocks: Both develop programming to solve problems. Groningen applies it specifically to numerical and physical problems.
Both develop single-variable calculus, including differentiation and integration. UCR also uses complex numbers and differential equations in a dynamic model.
Both directly study linear algebra, matrices, vector spaces and transformations.
Both use numerical algorithms to solve equations and differential equations. Groningen also applies statistics and machine learning to physics problems.
Both extend calculus for advanced quantitative work; UCR also covers complex functions and differential equations.
Both study discrete signals, sampling and the Z transform. UCR also treats continuous systems, Fourier analysis and feedback. Groningen goes further into quantisation and compressive sampling.
Both study waves and interference through practical work. Groningen develops a fuller mathematical and experimental sequence in electromagnetic waves and optics.

audience.programmeDescription: Applied Physics at the University of Groningen studies how physical principles can be used to design and measure technical systems. Students develop mathematical and experimental skills, study materials and devices, and complete an individual research project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers related study in quantitative modelling and robotics, Earth systems and energy, or biomedical systems and imaging. Groningen provides more depth in experimental physics, materials, device physics and instrumentation.
